items.title: Mcbee interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2020
items.q: when I played eventually played with Alice Coltrane. But what I’m thinking is it wasn’t me that created that bass line. Alice Coltrane showed me that bass line. “This is what I want you to play.”

ctx.x: Well my question is, moving from placing quarter notes and swing and playing on top of the beat, this was a totally different task for you it seems like, playing a bass line repetitively in some cases basically the similar thing all the way through, while other players did their explorations. Like you were the anchor. And I wonder if you enjoyed that role, for sometimes the songs could go on for eight or nine minutes. How do you keep your concentration?

You don’t concentrate, you just feel it. Something like that, by that I mean it’s just a vibe. You are now as a bassist, you are now being rather responsible to maintain the bass line that would support all that is happening beyond you melodically, harmonically, etcetera, etcetera. It was something, quite frankly, that I was already sort of familiar with. Number one my second group — my first group that I performed with in New York City was with Jackie McLean. He trained Bobby Hutcherson, Charles Tolliver, and…
This is sort of a personal question, do you feel you are a spiritual man? Does faith play a significant role in your life?

items.title: Mcbee interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2020
items.q: Occasionally I’d play a concert with Alice.

ctx.x: Yeah. Excellent. So when you got to New York we talked about you felt pretty good about your musicianship and it sounds to me like you had less of a struggle than a lot of other musicians. I don’t know if you can compare your experience to someone else, but you played from ’69 to ’72 if my facts are correct, both with Alice Coltrane and Pharoah Sanders simultaneously?
Mostly with Pharoah. I was in Pharoah’s band at the time. Occasionally I’d play a concert with Alice.
Can you describe, first, a recording session with Pharoah Sanders. What did you know beforehand, if anything, when you went to the session? Had you played the music live?

items.title: Mcbee interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2020
items.q: there was a lady whose name was Alice McLeod. She would have jam sessions at her big Victorian home every Sunday, which I would, you know, participate in occasionally.

ctx.x: Louis Hayes. I was sort of a, until now, an adopted son of Detroit, because people seem to have liked what I did. And so I got a chance to play with everybody. And you learn that, you know, at that particular time Detroit was the place where most of the great musicians, you know, came from, you know, Barry Harris, and — there was a vibe there, there was a lady whose name was Alice McLeod. She would have jam sessions at her big Victorian home every Sunday, which I would, you know, participate in occasionally.…
